\chapter*{The Telugu script --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Telugu script (reference)}
\markboth{Telugu script}{Telugu script}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — a place to look things up. You are \emph{not} meant to read this before the lessons: the lessons teach reading through real words, introducing each letter as a word needs it. This page just gathers the system in one spot.

\section*{How the Telugu script works (the three facts the lessons teach)}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Consonants carry a built-in \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.} \te{క} = \textquotedblleft{}ka,\textquotedblright{} \te{మ} = \textquotedblleft{}ma,\textquotedblright{} \te{ర} = \textquotedblleft{}ra.\textquotedblright{} (Many wear the \emph{talakaṭṭu}, a small check-mark hat.) You never write the short \emph{a}.
  \item \textbf{A vowel sign changes that built-in vowel.} Attached to a consonant it gives \te{కా} = kā · \te{కి} = ki · \te{కీ} = kī · \te{కు} = ku · \te{కూ} = kū · \te{కె} = ke · \te{కే} = kē · \te{కొ} = ko · \te{కో} = kō. The signs themselves are \textbf{\te{ా}} ā · \textbf{\te{ి}} i · \textbf{\te{ీ}} ī · \textbf{\te{ు}} u · \textbf{\te{ూ}} ū · \textbf{\te{ె}} e · \textbf{\te{ే}} ē · \textbf{\te{ొ}} o · \textbf{\te{ో}} ō.
  \item \textbf{A \emph{virama} (\te{్}) strips the vowel, and the bare consonant \emph{stacks below} the next as a conjunct.} \te{స్} + \te{క} $\to$ \te{స్క} (ska), \te{న్} + \te{య} $\to$ \te{న్య} (nya). A dot \textbf{anusvāra} (\te{ం}) adds a final nasal.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Independent vowels (word-initial)}

\textbf{\te{అ}} a · \textbf{\te{ఆ}} ā · \textbf{\te{ఇ}} i · \textbf{\te{ఈ}} ī · \textbf{\te{ఉ}} u · \textbf{\te{ఊ}} ū · \textbf{\te{ఎ}} e · \textbf{\te{ఏ}} ē · \textbf{\te{ఐ}} ai · \textbf{\te{ఒ}} o · \textbf{\te{ఓ}} ō · \textbf{\te{ఔ}} au.

\section*{Worth flagging}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Aspiration is written.} \te{క} k / \te{ఖ} kh, \te{గ} g / \te{ఘ} gh, \te{ద} d / \te{ధ} dh — the \textquotedblleft{}h\textquotedblright{} is a real puff. Like Kannada and unlike Tamil, Telugu keeps separate letters for the Sanskrit aspirates and voiced stops, because it borrowed so many Sanskrit words.
  \item \textbf{Round, looping forms.} Telugu and Kannada are script-sisters, shaped for palm-leaf writing; the two look far more alike than either does to Tamil.
  \item \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}The Italian of the East.\textquotedblright{}} Telugu words tend to end in vowels, giving the language an open, musical flow.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Telugu in the Dravidian family}

\textbf{Dravidian} is a family entirely separate from Indo-European (English, Latin, Sanskrit). Telugu shares grammar and native vocabulary with Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam — but, like Kannada and unlike Tamil, it borrowed \textbf{heavily} from Sanskrit. It also shows the family is not uniform: where its sisters say \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} with a word from the root \emph{il-} (\emph{illai / illa}), Telugu uses its own \emph{lēdu} / \emph{kādu}. The lessons trace, word by word, what is home-grown and what is borrowed.
